region: Capital city in Sao Tome and Principe
h1: Sao Tome travel, stays & events guide
heroText: Sao Tome is the compact seafront capital of Sao Tome and Principe, a Portuguese-colonial town wrapped in cocoa plantations and equatorial rainforest. First-time visitors should explore Fort São Sebastião's National Museum, admire the towers of the Sé Cathedral, and relax on the in-town sands of Praia Lagarto. São Tomé International Airport sits minutes from the centre, making this one of Africa's easiest island capitals to reach and explore on foot.

areas.name: Baixa (Historic Centre)
areas.text: Baixa is Sao Tome's colonial-era centre, packed with pastel administrative buildings, the fort, cathedral and central market, ideal for walking.

areas.name: Praia Lagarto
areas.text: Praia Lagarto is the city's in-town beach strip, lined with hotels and restaurants a short walk from the historic centre.

areas.name: Riboque
areas.text: Riboque is a quieter residential district east of the centre, home to embassies and guesthouses away from downtown traffic.

areas.name: Pantufo
areas.text: Pantufo is a fishing village on the coast just outside the city, good for fresh seafood and a slower pace by the water.

airports.name: São Tomé International Airport (TMS)
airports.search: São Tomé International Airport, São Tomé, Sao Tome and Principe
airports.text: São Tomé International Airport sits at the edge of the capital, a short taxi ride from downtown hotels and the Praia Lagarto beachfront.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between São Tomé International Airport (TMS) and central Sao Tome before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

bookingDestination: Sao Tome, Sao Tome and Principe
stayOverview: Base in Baixa for an easy first stay near the fort, cathedral and market, or choose Praia Lagarto for beachfront hotels a short walk from downtown. Riboque suits quieter stays near embassies, while Pantufo offers a slower, seafood-focused base by the water.
hotelIntro: Sao Tome hotel choice depends on priorities: Baixa suits first-time visitors wanting colonial architecture and museums within walking distance, Praia Lagarto suits beach-focused stays, and Riboque or Pantufo suit travelers wanting a quieter, more local base.
rentalCars: A rental car or driver is useful for reaching cocoa plantations and beaches around the island, since the small capital itself is easily walked.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Baixa or Praia Lagarto for an easy first stay within walking distance of the fort, cathedral and beachfront restaurants.

travelTips.title: Cocoa plantation trips
travelTips.text: Set aside a day to visit a roça such as Água Izé or Monte Café, the historic cocoa plantations that shaped the islands' economy.

travelTips.title: Airport convenience
travelTips.text: Take advantage of São Tomé International Airport's short distance from downtown, making even late arrivals straightforward.

travelTips.title: Currency and cash
travelTips.text: Carry Sao Tome and Principe dobras or euros for small purchases, since card acceptance is limited outside larger hotels.

nearbyIdeas.name: Roça Água Izé
nearbyIdeas.label: Heritage
nearbyIdeas.text: Roça Água Izé is a historic cocoa plantation east of the capital, with colonial-era buildings and a working rail line worth a guided visit.

nearbyIdeas.name: Ilhéu das Rolas
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Ilhéu das Rolas marks the equator line off the island's southern tip, a popular day trip for beaches and the symbolic crossing.

nearbyIdeas.name: Praia Jalé
nearbyIdeas.label: Beach
nearbyIdeas.text: Praia Jalé is a wide, dark-sand beach on the south coast, a scenic drive from the capital for swimming and turtle-nesting season.

history.text: The island was uninhabited before the arrival of the Portuguese sometime around 1470.
Álvaro Caminha founded the colony of São Tomé in 1493.

In 1497, 2,000 Jewish children, eight years old and under, were kidnapped from the Iberian peninsula, and forcefully converted to receive catholic education, following the national policy of conversion to Catholicism.
Another early building is Fort São Sebastião, built in 1566 and now the São Tomé National Museum.
On 9 July 1595, a slave revolt led by Rei Amador took control of the capital; they were subjugated in 1596.
In 1599, the Dutch took the city as well as the islands for two days; they re-occupied it in 1641 for a year.
The island of São Tomé was the main center of sugar production in the sixteenth century; it was overtaken by Brazil by 1600.

history.label: 19th century
history.text: São Tomé is centred on a sixteenth-century cathedral, that was largely rebuilt in the 19th century.
The city served as the capital of the Portuguese colony of São Tomé and Príncipe and, from São Tomé and Príncipe's independence in 1975, as capital of the sovereign nation.

history.label: Growth
history.text: The Portuguese came to São Tomé in search of land to grow sugarcane.

history.label: Civic role
history.text: The nearby African Kingdom of Kongo eventually became a source of slave labor as well.
